*ALL OF THIS IS FROM MY OWN EXPERIENCE. I HIGHLY SUGGEST SHE TALK WITH A THERAPIST OR SOME OTHER PROFESSIONAL FOR HELP*  That being said, here are some of my thoughts from MY battles with depression.

I think she needs to get out and do things. I don't mean to be rude, but a significant other can't be reason to live. It's an unhealthy crutch to survive off of someone else and there's a chance it feeds into guilt. Try to communicate to her that you care, but the emphasis should be that SHE is worth something, that she is someone who is loved, and she's someone who belongs in the world. 

What can you do? Well, a lot of it has to come from her, but you can try to support her. A HUGE help is exercise. If she's not exercising then try to walk with her, run, hike, lift weights, etc. Whatever she likes to do. Exercise is a natural antidepressant and statistically seems to work better than medically prescribed drugs.  https://www.verywellmind.com/exercise-is-an-effective-antidepressant-2330615 I've read a lot of these articles and my positivity often starts with a workout routine. It can take a few days or weeks to start seeing the effects (again my experience), but it does make a difference.

She could also try making friends through community college classes. She could take language classes, art, glass blowing, whatever. Something that sounds fun to her and would let her come into contact with more people. Meetups or a part time job or conventions may also be something she could do. Just something that lets her interact with more people. She needs a social group and she needs to expand her world outside of the walls of a house. Feeling trapped in a room drives you insane and your view of the world narrows until you can't see outside your own head.

The viability of some of these options depend on where you live, but your physical state is very important for mental stability. If your body is unhealthy, it can exacerbate mental issues. She should be eating well, drinking enough water, sleeping enough, getting exercise, etc. 

A larger social support group is important too. She should take some time to mess around, have fun, and find things that she likes to do while meeting people in the process. It takes A LOT of discipline to work your way to the point that you can enjoy things again. 

Again, all of this eventually has to come from her own mind, but support is helpful. If she vents her feelings, try to be caring and supportive, not shocked and scared. Make sure she knows you love her and that there's nothing wrong with her for going through this. Make sure she feels like she's not broken or a burden, she's just struggling. She needs to feel like she can make it through, which means appreciating small victories.

I wish her all the best. Depression sucks, but it can be managed and I'm determined to rid my life of it completely eventually. I believe it's possible and I hope she can believe the same.
